title: When Dissent Becomes “Terror”
author: Henry Giroux
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2024/05/IMG_6768-680x510.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/20/when-
dissent-becomes-terror/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2024/05/IMG_6768-680x510.jpeg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

> Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently
>
> – Rosa Luxemburg****

[Every democracy worthy of the name recognizes a simple but indispensable
truth](https://freedomhouse.org/report/freedom-world/2022/global-expansion-
authoritarian-rule): dissent is not its enemy but its lifeblood. The freedom
to criticize those in power, expose injustice, challenge entrenched authority,
organize collectively, and imagine a more just future is the foundation upon
which a meaningful democratic society rests. Without the right to dissent,
citizenship becomes obedience, violence is normalized, politics collapses into
spectacle, corrupt power is legitimated, reason disappears into an abyss of
lies, and freedom is reduced to little more than an empty slogan. In such a
society, state violence no longer needs to hide in the shadows; [it is
transformed into theater, a public spectacle of fear, humiliation, and
degradation.](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/02/the-theater-of-
punishment/)

Authoritarianism begins by reversing democracy's foundational principle. It
does not merely silence critics; it first rewrites the language through which
people understand politics itself. Protest becomes disorder. Journalism
becomes subversion. Critical education becomes indoctrination. Independent
thought becomes disloyalty. Memory becomes dangerous. Manufactured ignorance
is elevated over literacy precisely because literacy offers the possibility of
agency. Citizens who refuse to submit are defined as extremists, traitors, or
terrorists. Fascism emerges as a regime of regulated memory[, imposing
pedagogical structures that dictate what can be known, what must be remembered
or forgotten, and what is permitted to be mourned or
celebrated](https://www.cumhuriyet.com.tr/yazarlar/ergin-yildizoglu/fasizm-ve-
kultur-2415735). Before authoritarian regimes imprison bodies, they colonize
consciousness, imposing a cultural and pedagogical regime organized around
racism, bigotry, greed, isolation, and apocalyptic visions. They teach people
to fear dissent more than concentrated power, to mistake obedience for
patriotism, and ultimately to embrace repression as the price of security.

This assault on democratic consciousness never relies on police power alone.
Every authoritarian movement understands that force can suppress opposition
temporarily, but only culture’s pedagogical power can make domination appear
natural. As a result, authoritarian politics wages war not only through
courts, prisons, and executive decrees but also through schools, universities,
libraries, museums, the arts, the media, religious institutions, digital
platforms, and every cultural apparatus capable of shaping public memory,
civic identity, and moral responsibility. Democracy is won or lost not only
through elections and laws but also through education, culture, language, and
the stories a society tells about itself. As [John Dewey argued in Freedom and
Culture](https://www.simonandschuster.ca/books/Freedom-and-Culture/John-
Dewey/9780879755607), a vibrant democracy depends upon a civic culture—a
pedagogical matrix of habits, dispositions, and sensibilities—that ensures its
survival. When that culture embraces anti-democratic values and visions while
destroying the social fabric that binds people together, the formative
conditions that cultivate critical agency and democratic citizenship begin to
disappear. The consequences are not merely cultural; they become visible in
the institutions, policies, and practices through which authoritarian power is
organized and dissent is repressed.

The criminalization of dissent and the violent repression of protesters [have
long accompanied moments of democratic crisis in the United
States](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.ca/books/770181/a-protest-history-of-
the-united-states-by-gloria-j-browne-marshall/9780807010815). The Trump regime
distinguishes itself by the scale, brazenness, and ideological coherence with
which it has revived this tradition. Even more revealing, we are witnessing
one of the most aggressive campaigns in generations to criminalize dissent
while transforming the institutions of culture into the pedagogical machinery
of authoritarianism.

The ambitions of this project extend far beyond partisan politics. It seeks to
normalize state violence, legitimize the concentration of executive power,
erase historical memory, and redefine [democratic opposition as a form of
domestic terrorism](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-
reports/trumps-orders-targeting-antifascism-aim-criminalize-opposition). Its
goal is not simply to govern citizens but to reshape how they think, what they
remember, whom they fear, and what they are willing to accept as normal. [As
the Lemkin Institute](https://www.lemkininstitute.com/statements-new-
page/statement-on-the-normalization-of-nazism-in-
the-u.s-government?utm_campaign=6b5c3c5e-e9) has warned, Trump’s attack on
democratic institutions and those who defend them is part of a broader process
of normalization sustained by “a language and symbolism rooted in genocidal
ideology, dulling collective awareness of its harms and desensitizing society
to its violence.”

[That project came into sharp focus when Secretary of State Marco Rubio
convened an international summit devoted to what the Trump administration
described as the global threat of "far-left
terrorism."](https://www.commondreams.org/news/stephen-miller-nspm-7) Joined
by White House adviser Stephen Miller, one of the administration’s most
fanatical white nationalist ideologues, Rubio warned of an international
menace supposedly posed by left-wing movements while portraying political
opponents as enemies of civilization whose claims to constitutional
protections deserved little consideration. Embracing the dehumanizing language
of the [McCarthy era](https://www.ellenschrecker.com/theageofmccarthyism),
Rubio dismissed the left as animated by “[a poisonous resentment cloaked in
the language of equality, justice, and liberation” [describing its adherents
as people driven by] “an overwhelming need to tear down, to wreck what is
beautiful and what is right.”](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/jul/16/political-violence-event-trump-marco-rubio) He concluded with
a familiar nationalist refrain: “They despise the West because the West is
great.”

Such language does more than vilify political opponents. Resurrecting the
language of the Confederacy and the blood-and-soil rhetoric of racial-
purification movements, this discourse casts immigrants as a civilizational
threat; that is[, a contaminating presence allegedly poisoning the nation’s
blood](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/trump-says-immigrants-
are-poisoning-blood-country-biden-campaign-liken-rcna130141), undermining its
racial purity, and threatening the imagined supremacy of a white Christian
America. The purpose is not merely to exclude immigrants but to redefine
democratic citizenship through a racist logic that treats difference as
contamination and resistance as political subversion. Those marked as foreign
are cast outside the protection of the nation, while those who defend them are
branded enemies from within. Rubio’s disingenuousness takes one’s breath away,
embodied in a death-dealing rhetoric that feeds on its own moral rot, strips
language of conscience, and embraces cruelty without hesitation, remorse, or
shame.

[Stephen Miller's hysterical remarks revealed the deeper ideological
architecture of this project](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/jul/16/political-violence-event-trump-marco-rubio). He claimed that
the left is driven by envy and hatred of “a perfect family with a perfect life
and a perfect job and a perfect kid and goes [sic] to church every Sunday.”
Beneath this sentimental Disneyified image lies a project of racial cleansing
parading as a political ideal: a white Christian nationalist vision of America
in which immigrants, people of color, journalists, critical educators, student
protesters, and anyone who challenges state power become enemies of the nation
itself. Miller’s racialized nostalgia for the patriarchal family echoes [Jack
Luzkow’s](https://nexus-instituut.nl/en/essay/fighting-fascism-at-the-
apocalypse) observation that Trump’s vision of America “comes in the name of
the Flag, the cross, and nostalgia. It comes because of the fear of the
future, the fear that white Christians are being displaced by Muslims and
Mexicans, the fear of irreversible decline, the fear of China, the fear of
technology and the robots that are coming for American jobs.” It is an
authoritarian vision that [Zeteo senior politics editor Andrew Perez has aptly
described as “characteristically apocalyptic and
authoritarian](https://zeteo.com/p/stephen-miller-expands-his-apocalyptic),”
one that enables Miller to live out what Perez calls his “violent fantasy.”
Within this morally decrepit universe, the separation of migrant families, the
expansion of privately operated ICE detention centers, the abduction of
students, and U.S. complicity in the mass killing of civilians in Gaza and
Lebanon become either necessary acts of national defense or objects of
indifference, while those who condemn such policies are branded extremists.

What is at work here is more than the delusional fiction of fanatical
certainty and moral self-righteousness; it is an abject political illiteracy
joined to a profound thoughtlessness, evident in the overt and self-conscious
destruction of every vestige of humanity. Nowhere is this fascist logic of
ethical corruption more apparent than in Miller’s portrayal of ICE agents as
the real victims in Trump’s white Christian nationalist warfare state. In
reality, as [Andrew Perez](https://zeteo.com/p/stephen-miller-expands-his-
apocalyptic) points out, these are “violent, masked thugs who kidnap people,
terrorize communities, and kill immigrants and U.S. citizens alike.” This is
moral nihilism in its most dangerous form: a cultivated political
thoughtlessness that refuses the claims of conscience and makes the
destruction of human beings easier to ignore, justify, or celebrate. Miller
thus defends a growing paramilitary force steeped in white supremacist
ideology, one whose agents have exchanged the white robes of racial terror for
the uniforms and machinery of authoritarian power. In this political order,
cruelty becomes policy, suffering becomes spectacle, and the destruction of
empathy is elevated into a civic virtue. It is a politics that wages war on
the very meaning of our shared humanity.

ICE, now the most heavily funded law enforcement agency in the Trump
administration, is not merely an agency of immigration control. It is the
institutional spearhead of what Eddie Glaude Jr. identifies as a restorative
project, one designed to reclaim America as a white republic. The policing of
migrants cannot be separated from this larger politics of racial restoration.
Within this project, exclusion, disposability, and state violence become the
instruments for reconstructing a nation defined by white Christian
nationalism. In such a political order, cruelty becomes policy, suffering
becomes spectacle, and the destruction of empathy is elevated into a civic
virtue. It is a politics that wages war on the very meaning of our shared
humanity.

[Border czar Tom
Homan](https://x.com/atrupar/status/2077756329821610159?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E2077756329821610159%7Ctwgr%5Ee5b56df623d2f0),
appearing on Fox News, extended this logic even further, repeatedly suggesting
that Democratic politicians who resist the administration's immigration
policies are aiding terrorists or behaving like terrorists themselves. Even
worse, he stated that “It all go backs **[sic]** to the Dems … there's still
gonna be more bloodshed unless they shut their mouth and let ICE enforce the
laws that they enacted.” Here fascist politics reveals its final truth: the
victims of state violence disappear, those who protest their suffering are
blamed for the violence inflicted upon them, and the perpetrators proclaim
themselves innocent. What disappears most completely in Homan's account is the
humanity of those whose lives have been shattered or destroyed. They vanish
into the bloodless abstractions of "enforcement," leaving behind only a
political narrative designed to absolve the state and criminalize its critics.

Rubio, Miller, and Homan are dangerous not only because they are white
supremacists and ideological fanatics, but because they wield the machinery of
the state, its powers of education, repression, surveillance, and
disposability. Their rhetoric exemplifies what [Pankaj
Mishra](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250159304/ageofanger/) identifies
as the “cult of redemptive violence,” a politics in which brutality is not
merely tolerated but endowed with the moral force of purification and renewal.
The cumulative effect of this rhetoric is unmistakable. Political disagreement
is now viewed as evidence of criminality and national betrayal, and therefore
as justification for state violence.

Taken together, this rhetoric constitutes a politics of fear, degradation, and
violence. Its purpose is not merely to silence opposition but to reshape
citizens into compliant subjects, teaching them to mistake intimidation for
security, humiliation for justice, and cruelty for civic virtue. State
violence is redefined as virtue, dissent is transformed into terrorism**.**
[History teaches that such dehumanizing narratives are never merely
rhetorical](https://www.simonandschuster.ca/books/Erasing-History/Jason-
Stanley/9781668056929). They prepare the cultural and moral conditions in
which persecution, repression, and eventually mass violence become thinkable
and, all too often, publicly acceptable. What follows is a descent into a
moral abyss in which cruelty loses its power to shock and the unthinkable is
normalized.

This politics of moral annihilation is reinforced by the administration’s
revival of Cold War hysteria. The hysterical anti-communism driving the Trump
administration is on full display in the remarks of Rubio, Miller, and others.
As[Robert Koehler](https://www.laprogressive.com/election-and-
campaigns/communists-will-kill-
you?utm_source=LA+Progressive+NEW&utm_campaign=4af74ed8c2-LAP_News_4_15_April_17_PC4_15_2017_COPY_01&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_61288e16ef-4af74ed8c2-1256770390&mc_cid=4af74ed8c2&mc_eid=8b5140483e)
observes, with Democratic socialists on the rise, Trump and his minions resort
to “fear-mongering [as] a cover for his administration’s fear-creating. It’s
not godless communists who are walking around, arresting and sometimes killing
Americans, it’s the Trump Gestapo, also known as ICE.”

These statements reveal far more than rhetorical excess. They expose an
emerging governing philosophy. The significance of Rubio's, Miller's, and
Homan's remarks lies not simply in their rhetorical excesses but in what they
reveal about the administration's broader political strategy. Democratic
dissent is being recast as a national security threat, while the language of
counterterrorism is increasingly deployed against critics of the state rather
than against those who undermine democracy through violence. Homan’s response
to the ICE killings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Johan Sebastian
Guerrero in Maine made this strategy brutally clear: state officials defend
the agents responsible, blame Democrats and protesters for the bloodshed, and
then invoke the violence they have helped produce as grounds for silencing
further criticism.

The omissions were as revealing as the accusations. Neither Rubio nor Miller
devoted serious attention to the January 6 assault on the United States
Capitol, the most direct attack on the peaceful transfer of presidential power
in modern American history. They did not object to Trump’s pardoning of the
rioters, including those who brutally assaulted Capitol police officers, nor
did they confront the [extensive record of violence committed by white
supremacist and other far-right extremist
movements](https://www.journalofdemocracy.org/articles/the-rise-of-political-
violence-in-the-united-states/), long identified by researchers as among the
most persistent sources of domestic political violence in the United States.
Such selective outrage is more than hypocrisy. It reflects an authoritarian
logic in which state violence and right-wing extremism are erased from public
view, while democratic resistance becomes the principal source of political
danger.

The consequences of this distortion reach far beyond political rhetoric, for
its logic is increasingly embedded in public policy. The expansion of
militarized immigration enforcement, the deployment of federal forces into
American cities, the escalating use of surveillance powers, the broad claims
advanced under [National Security Presidential
Memorandum-7](https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/how-nspm-7-seeks-to-
use-domestic-terrorism-to-target-nonprofits-and-activists), the increasingly
severe prosecution of protesters all point toward a common objective:
narrowing the space in which democratic opposition can exist while expanding
the reach of the national security state. [The shocking sentences imposed on
protesters in Texas](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/26/texas-
protesters-anti-ice-convictions) reveal the increasingly punitive machinery
being deployed against dissent, demonstrating how the power of the state can
be mobilized not simply to control protest but to intimidate those who dare to
challenge its authority.

Alongside these legal and political developments, the administration has
intensified its assault on the institutions that sustain democratic culture.
[Universities face political intimidation and threats to their
funding;](https://www.developmenteducationreview.com/issue/issue-42/higher-
education-time-fascist-plague) public schools are pressured to censor history
and silence teachers; [libraries confront organized campaigns to remove
books](https://americanlibrariesmagazine.org/2025/03/19/tracking-the-trump-
administrations-attacks-on-libraries/); [museums are pushed to sanitize the
nation’s past](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/06/us/politics/trump-
smithsonian-ideological-fight.html); and journalists and [independent media
are vilified as enemies](https://www.versobooks.com/en-
ca/products/214-scorched-
earth?srsltid=AfmBOoq2IwAYtJpwDGJgtC0FPyv1w6qmKMssjQTPuGq4PVuSI2su6ugt). Taken
together, these attacks seek to capture the institutions through which
societies produce knowledge, preserve memory, and cultivate informed judgment,
making authoritarianism appear not exceptional but inevitable.

The danger before us is therefore larger than any single administration or
policy. What has emerged is a political culture in which democracy itself is
redefined as a threat whenever citizens dare to hold power accountable. Once
governments succeed in persuading people that dissent is terrorism, solidarity
is conspiracy, journalism is sedition, education is indoctrination, and
justice is disorder, the foundations of democratic life begin to erode from
within. History reminds us that democracies rarely disappear overnight. They
are dismantled gradually as fear replaces hope, cruelty replaces compassion,
propaganda replaces truth, and obedience replaces civic courage.

The defense of dissent is therefore about far more than protecting the rights
of protesters or journalists. More fundamentally, it is about preserving the
civic imagination upon which a meaningful democracy depends. Every generation
must decide whether it will surrender the language of freedom to those who
govern through fear or reclaim the democratic conviction that questioning
power, defending truth, and standing in solidarity with others are not crimes
but the highest responsibilities of free people. What is ultimately at stake
is far more than policies or elections. It is whether democracy can survive as
a lived culture rather than be hollowed out into the political facade of
gangster capitalism, where concentrated wealth governs through fear,
disposability, corruption, and organized cruelty while democratic institutions
remain only as empty shells. Democracy cannot survive when it becomes
synonymous with the rule of oligarchs, the commodification of every public
value, and the substitution of market power for civic responsibility. It
survives only as a culture capable of nurturing informed judgment, collective
responsibility, and the courage to imagine a future beyond authoritarian rule.
To grasp how such a politics takes hold, however, we must first examine the
machinery of dehumanization through which authoritarian power acquires its
legitimacy, emotional force, and capacity to make the unthinkable appear
ordinary.

**The Politics of Moral Collapse**

The criminalization of dissent depends upon a deeper moral reversal.
Authoritarian politics does not deny violence; it relocates it. Violence
exercised by the state is recast as law, order, patriotism, or national
security, while those who expose injustice or challenge abuses of power are
portrayed as dangerous extremists. Under this logic, heavily armed federal
agents carrying out militarized immigration raids are defenders of public
safety, while students marching against injustice, journalists investigating
government misconduct, teachers defending historical truth, and citizens
protesting unconstitutional policies become the true enemies of the nation.
Violence is no longer judged by what it does but by who exercises it.

This authoritarian logic now shapes the expanding machinery of state power in
the United States. [The administration has repeatedly justified the deployment
of federal troops and tactical forces into American cities while presenting
such extraordinary measures as necessary acts of public
protection](https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/trumps-expanded-
domestic-military-use-should-worry-us-all). It has vastly expanded the powers
of immigration enforcement, unleashing ICE as an increasingly militarized arm
of state terror while defending its raids, abductions, detentions, and deadly
violence through the fascist language of invasion, contamination, and
permanent emergency. [Within this authoritarian imaginary, often
spectacularized,]() immigrants are .transformed into enemy populations whose
persecution becomes public spectacle, masked agents operate with expanding
impunity, and constitutional safeguards are redefined as intolerable obstacles
to the exercise of unchecked state power.

The fatal shooting of Johan Sebastian Guerrero during an ICE operation cannot
be dismissed as an isolated tragedy or bureaucratically sanitized as the
unfortunate consequence of "enforcement." It also exposes precisely what
Homan's rhetoric erases: the humanity of those destroyed by state violence.
[As Jeffrey St. Clair's](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/16/why-did-they-
shoot-him/) moving portrait makes clear, Guerrero was not an abstraction or a
statistic but a young man remembered for his generosity, dignity, and deep
devotion to his family and community. His life stands as a rebuke to the
official language that reduces human beings to targets, suspects, or
collateral damage. This is how authoritarianism works: it destroys people
physically only after it has rendered them politically invisible and morally
disposable. The killing of Guerrero belongs to a widening landscape of state
violence in which human beings are rendered disposable, terror is normalized
as public policy, and the machinery of repression is concealed behind the
bloodless vocabulary of law, order, and "enforcement." Nor can the human cost
of this system be dismissed: [since Trump began his second term, at least 51
people have died in ICE custody](https://truthout.org/articles/ice-
says-51-people-died-in-custody-under-trump-experts-say-thats-an-undercount/),
a figure experts warn may significantly undercount the actual toll. Lives are
lost, families are devastated, communities are terrorized, yet accountability
is too often replaced by bureaucratic rationalizations and political
indifference.

At the same time, the administration has intensified its effort to criminalize
democratic resistance. NSPM-7 marks an alarming expansion of the national
security state under the banner of combating domestic extremism,
[criminalizing dissent through a sweeping executive directive issued without
congressional approval](https://theconversation.com/the-trump-administrations-
global-campaign-against-radical-left-terrorism-is-built-on-a-national-
security-memo-without-congressional-approval-287276)**.** [Civil liberties
advocates have warned that its broad language risks collapsing the distinction
between violent acts and constitutionally protected political
activity](https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/how-nspm-7-seeks-to-use-
domestic-terrorism-to-target-nonprofits-and-activists), granting federal
authorities unprecedented latitude to monitor, investigate, and prosecute
individuals and organizations whose principal offense is opposition to
government policy. History teaches that when governments acquire expansive
powers in the name of security, those powers rarely remain confined to genuine
threats. They almost inevitably migrate toward those who challenge existing
relations of power.

That danger is no longer hypothetical. Across the country, protesters are
facing increasingly aggressive prosecutions under conspiracy statutes and
terrorism-related theories once largely reserved for organized criminal
enterprises. [The extraordinary sentences imposed on anti-ICE protesters in
Texas](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/26/texas-protesters-anti-
ice-convictions) shocked legal observers precisely because they signaled
something far more ominous than the punishment of individual wrongdoing: the
emergence of a system of repression willing to collapse political association
into criminal conspiracy and recast democratic protest as organized extremism.
Nor is Texas an isolated case. In Minnesota, federal prosecutors have brought
conspiracy charges against activists accused of organizing resistance to the
administration’s immigration crackdown**.**[Federal authorities have also
pursued scores of cases against protesters in Los Angeles, Portland, Chicago,
and Washington, D.C](https://www.usnews.com/news/us/articles/2025-12-18/key-
findings-of-an-ap-analysis-examining-federal-prosecutions-of-protesters).,
often accompanying these prosecutions with rhetoric that portrays political
opposition as extremism. Here the legal architecture of the authoritarian
state comes fully into view**:** the line between dissent and criminality is
deliberately erased and opposition to state power is increasingly redefined as
conspiracy, subversion, and even terrorism. This is how repression acquires
the force of law: the dissenter becomes the criminal, the protester becomes
the enemy, and the exercise of democratic freedom itself becomes grounds for
surveillance, prosecution, and punishment.

The administration's attack on democratic opposition extends beyond the
courtroom[. Journalists investigating abuses of power have encountered
escalating intimidation, exclusion, legal threats, and public
denunciation](https://apnews.com/article/trump-administration-media-new-york-
times-a1100f027095e07ffb5fbd1708e70942). Independent reporting, once
understood as indispensable to holding power accountable, is increasingly
depicted as an obstacle to national unity or as an enemy of the people. Trump
recently offered a revealing display of authoritarian power fused with wounded
vanity [when, after ABC and NBC refused to broadcast his speech on alleged
voter fraud, he suggested that their broadcast licenses should be
revoked](https://www.cato.org/blog/broadcasters-should-not-lose-their-
licenses-because-they-dont-broadcast-presidents-
speech?utm_source=hootsuite&utm_medium=facebook&utm_term=&utm_content=&utm_campaign=).
The episode would be laughable if it were not so dangerous: a president,
enraged that television networks declined to provide the national audience he
believed he was owed, invoked the regulatory power of government as an
instrument of political revenge. Here the petulance of the autocrat merges
with the logic of authoritarian rule, the childish demand to be seen and
obeyed, backed by the menacing power to punish those who refuse. The objective
is not merely to silence particular reporters or intimidate individual
networks but to undermine the independence of every institution capable of
exposing governmental deception, corruption, and abuse. When citizens no
longer trust independent sources of information, they become increasingly
dependent upon official narratives, political spectacle, and propaganda.

Yet these developments cannot be understood simply as attacks on individual
institutions. They reveal a broader authoritarian strategy aimed at
reorganizing public consciousness itself. Authoritarian rule requires far more
than obedient laws; it requires citizens whose moral imaginations have been
reshaped to accept repression as common sense. For that reason, its primary
target is not any single institution but the democratic capacities those
institutions cultivate: historical memory, critical judgment, civic literacy,
ethical responsibility, and the ability to distinguish truth from propaganda.
Once those capacities are weakened, citizens become increasingly vulnerable to
fear, manufactured ignorance, and political manipulation. The objective is not
merely to silence dissent but to transform the cultural conditions under which
dissent can even be imagined.

These attacks are often discussed separately, as disputes over education,
immigration, journalism, policing, or public safety. As I have argued
elsewhere, [such fragmentation obscures the comprehensive project taking
shape.](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10714413.2023.2243203)
Each assault reinforces the others, narrowing the spaces in which democratic
consciousness can develop and weakening the critical thought, historical
memory, compassion, and collective responsibility that make democracy
possible. Citizens deprived of the language **needed** to recognize injustice
become far easier to govern through fear.

Accordingly, the current assault on dissent cannot be reduced to debates over
law enforcement or public order. At stake is the struggle over political
imagination itself. Every authoritarian regime seeks not only to discipline
bodies but also to colonize the political imagination and narrow the
boundaries of what people believe is possible**.** It strives to convince
ordinary people that repression is freedom, ignorance is common sense, and
obedience is the highest form of patriotism. Democracy begins to die not only
when citizens lose their rights but when they lose the capacity to imagine
that another future remains possible. This assault on democratic consciousness
is not confined to the United States; it belongs to a global authoritarian
formation whose movements increasingly share the same language, strategies,
and political ambitions.

**The Global Grammar of Twenty-First-Century Fascism**

The current trajectory of the United States is neither exceptional nor
accidental. It is part of a broader authoritarian insurgency that has spread
across the globe, adapting itself to different national histories while
relying on a remarkably consistent political vocabulary. Whether in Hungary,
India, Argentina, Italy, El Salvador, Russia, or elsewhere, contemporary
authoritarian movements share a common grammar of power. They attack the
legitimacy of independent journalism, weaken universities, censor teachers and
public schools, rewrite national history, demonize immigrants and racialized
communities, vilify intellectuals and artists, concentrate executive
authority, militarize public life, and portray democratic critics as enemies
of the nation. They cultivate fear, elevate cruelty into a political virtue,
and transform insecurity into an instrument of governance.

These regimes differ in important respects, but they are united by a common
ambition: to replace the language of democracy with the language of fear.
Across national boundaries, democratic institutions are hollowed out while
retaining their outward appearance, historical memory is subordinated to
nationalist mythology, and citizens are encouraged to distrust evidence and
critical thought in favor of manufactured outrage and charismatic authority.
Democracy is emptied of its substance even as its symbols are cynically
appropriated.

What binds these developments together is not merely a shared politics but a
shared pedagogy. [Twenty-first-century fascism governs less by commanding
obedience than by producing forms of common sense that render domination
natural, cruelty virtuous, and democratic values
suspect](https://www.bloomsbury.com/ca/fascism-on-trial-9781350421684/). It
wages a relentless struggle over memory, language, desire, and everyday life,
[flooding digital culture with disinformation, transforming spectacle into a
substitute for reasoned public
debate](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/19/elon-musk-and-the-politics-of-
trillionaire-fascism/), and teaching citizens to distrust one another, forget
their histories, and equate compassion with weakness. Its deepest achievement
lies not simply in silencing opposition but in reshaping the moral and
political imagination before repression ever becomes fully visible, producing
subjects who no longer recognize authoritarianism when it arrives clothed in
the language of patriotism, security, and freedom.

This explains why schools, universities, libraries, museums, journalism, and
the arts have become central battlegrounds. These institutions cultivate
informed judgment, the capacity to distinguish truth from propaganda, a
culture of questioning, the ability to distinguish memory from myth, justice
from vengeance, and shared responsibility from organized selfishness. They
remind citizens that democracy is not inherited but learned, defended,
renewed, and expanded by every generation. For authoritarian movements, they
represent a profound danger precisely because they nurture the critical
consciousness and collective agency that make domination more difficult.

[The assault on these institutions is inseparable from the assault on
dissent](https://www.bloomsbury.com/ca/assassins-of-memory-9781350553521/)
because both are aimed at transforming the conditions under which people
think, judge, and act politically. Authoritarianism triumphs not when
criticism is merely silenced, but when citizens lose the capacity to recognize
domination itself. By the time democratic freedoms survive only as
constitutional forms emptied of civic substance, the work of authoritarian
education is already well underway.

This global convergence reveals not only the spread of authoritarian politics
but the emergence of a new institutional architecture of fascist power. Unlike
the classic fascist regimes of the twentieth century, the new authoritarianism
rarely arrives through military coups or the immediate abolition of elections.
It advances incrementally through legislatures, executive orders, courts,
media conglomerates, digital platforms, billionaire patronage, and the gradual
capture of educational and cultural institutions. Rather than destroying
democratic institutions outright, it empties them of their democratic
substance while preserving their outward forms, allowing authoritarian rule to
cloak itself in the language of constitutional order, national security, and
popular sovereignty. Its greatest institutional achievement is to normalize
this process, making the slow dismantling of democracy appear as its very
defense.

Beneath these institutional changes lies a deeper historical truth. Fascism
today is not simply the negation of democracy. It is the political form that
gangster capitalism assumes when even limited democratic demands begin to
threaten the concentration of wealth and power. [As Prabhat Patnaik
notes,](https://bostonreview.net/class-inequality-politics/prabhat-patnaik-
why-neoliberalism-needs-neofascists) when neoliberalism (gangster capitalism)
defaults on its promises of social mobility and a better life, it turns to
neofascism. When democratic institutions become obstacles to oligarchic rule,
they are hollowed out, privatized, militarized, and increasingly governed
through the language of permanent emergency. Under such conditions,
authoritarianism is no longer an aberration. It becomes the preferred
political instrument through which concentrated economic power protects itself
from democratic accountability.

Against this authoritarian convergence, the defense of democracy must be
fought across every institution in which people learn, remember, deliberate,
and act collectively. It cannot be confined to elections, court decisions, or
legislative battles alone. It must also be fought across the institutions of
education and culture, within labor and community organizations, and in every
public space where people learn to think critically, care for one another, and
imagine a future beyond fear. A socialist democracy can only emerge and
survive when it is sustained by a vibrant civic culture capable of resisting
the politics of disposability, organized forgetting, and manufactured
ignorance. The struggle before us is therefore not only political; it is
educational, cultural, moral, and profoundly international. Yet the global
advance of authoritarianism cannot be explained by captured institutions and
concentrated power alone. Its durability depends on its capacity to enter
everyday life, reshape ordinary relationships, and educate people into
accepting domination as common sense.

**Teaching Fascism: The Socialization of Everyday Life**

One of the most dangerous misconceptions about fascism is the belief that it
begins with concentration camps, secret police, or the formal abolition of
democratic institutions. By the time those horrors become visible, fascism has
already achieved one of its most important victories. It has transformed
everyday life into a vast educational force that teaches people how to think,
whom to fear, what to forget, and whose suffering no longer matters.

Contemporary fascism is best understood not simply as a political movement or
a set of governmental policies. Before anything else, it is an educational
project. Long before it governs through laws, prisons, and military force, [it
governs through culture](https://jacobin.com/2025/05/pepe-mujica-uruguay-
capitalism-solidarity). It wages a relentless struggle over language, memory,
desire, identity, and common sense. It seeks to reshape the moral imagination
by normalizing cruelty, celebrating ignorance, rewarding conformity, and
teaching citizens that democratic values, critical thought, compassion,
solidarity, equality, and dissent are signs of weakness rather than sources of
civic strength. [It also reproduces through culture anti-democratic habits
that sustain capitalism and undermine the social
fabric.](http://bostonreview.net/politics/melvin-rogers-democracy-habit-
practice-it)

This pedagogical machinery operates across the institutions that organize
everyday life. Schools replace honest history with nationalist mythology;
universities are disciplined through political intimidation and financial
coercion; libraries and museums become targets of censorship and historical
erasure; journalism is denounced as an enemy; and billionaire-owned media and
digital platforms transform politics into a permanent spectacle of resentment,
conspiracy, and distraction. Churches sanctify exclusion rather than
compassion, while entertainment industries glorify violence, hypermasculinity,
and the survival-of-the-fittest ethic of gangster capitalism. Across these
cultural sites, citizens are taught the same lesson: democracy is dangerous
because it encourages people to question authority, while authoritarianism
offers the comforting illusion of certainty, order, and belonging.

Its pedagogical reach extends deeply into everyday life, reshaping the most
basic human relationships. Fear replaces trust. Competition replaces
solidarity. Public problems become private failures. Compassion is ridiculed
as weakness. Cruelty becomes a spectacle to be consumed rather than resisted.
People begin to experience the humiliation of immigrants, the suffering of the
poor, the censorship of teachers, the harassment of journalists, and the
imprisonment of political opponents not as democratic emergencies but as
ordinary features of public life. The extraordinary becomes routine. The
unthinkable becomes thinkable. Eventually, it becomes acceptable.

Rubio’s summit, Miller’s rhetoric, the militarization of immigration
enforcement, the prosecution of protesters, and the attacks on education and
journalism are not disconnected responses to isolated crises. They form a
single pedagogical project, a regime of cultural violence, designed to make
authoritarian rule appear natural, necessary, and inevitable. Together, they
produce a form of civic illiteracy in which the public loses the capacity to
distinguish democracy from domination, freedom from fear, and justice from
revenge. If fascism educates people into resignation, fear, and cruelty,
resistance must do more than oppose its policies. It must cultivate the
solidarities, capacities, and political imagination necessary to build a
radically different future.

**Beyond Resistance: Reclaiming the Radical Democratic Imagination**

Every authoritarian movement seeks to convince people that there is no
alternative to fear, cruelty, permanent insecurity, and concentrated power.
The greatest victory of fascist politics is not simply that it suppresses
dissent but that it destroys the capacity to imagine a different future. It
teaches resignation instead of hope, cynicism instead of solidarity, and
private survival instead of collective struggle.

The answer cannot be a nostalgic return to the neoliberal order whose
inequalities, exclusions, and betrayals helped produce the conditions in which
contemporary fascism could flourish. Neoliberalism did not simply weaken
democratic institutions; it hollowed out the public sphere, reduced
citizenship to consumerism, celebrated privatization as freedom, normalized
staggering inequalities of wealth and power, and abandoned the very language
of the common good. It created a society in which democracy became
increasingly subordinate to the imperatives of capital long before
authoritarian movements openly sought to dismantle what remained.

The struggle before us is no longer simply a choice between authoritarian
capitalism and the increasingly hollow institutions of liberal democracy. More
fundamentally, it is a struggle between authoritarian capitalism and a radical
democratic politics committed to democratizing every major institution that
shapes everyday life, the economy no less than education, the workplace no
less than government, culture no less than elections. Democracy cannot survive
where economic power remains beyond democratic control, because concentrated
wealth inevitably seeks concentrated political power. Political democracy
without economic democracy remains permanently vulnerable to authoritarian
capture. The struggle against fascism is therefore inseparable from the
struggle against neoliberal capitalism at home and abroad. In its gangster
capitalist form, capitalism no longer merely corrodes democracy from within;
it increasingly generates the authoritarian forces that seek to replace it
altogether.

The alternative must be a fundamentally different democratic horizon informed
by the principles of radical democracy and democratic socialism**.** Such a
democracy places human needs above the imperatives of capital, expands rather
than contracts the public sphere, deepens democratic participation throughout
society, and recognizes education as the foundation of democratic freedom
rather than an instrument of conformity. It measures freedom not by the wealth
accumulated by a privileged few but by the degree to which all people possess
the political, economic, educational, cultural, and social capacities
necessary to exercise meaningful agency over the conditions of their lives.
Such a democracy does more than protect civil liberties. It creates the
material conditions that make freedom possible, insisting that freedom without
equality becomes privilege, equality without freedom becomes domination, and
both lose their emancipatory promise when detached from solidarity, historical
memory, and shared responsibility.

The struggle before us, then, is not simply to resist fascism but to build the
democratic socialist future that fascism fears most: a society in which power
is shared, wealth is democratized, education cultivates critical agency rather
than civic conformity, and every person is recognized as capable of shaping
the conditions of collective life. Against the authoritarian pedagogy that
saturates everyday life—teaching fear instead of hope, disposability instead
of solidarity, obedience instead of critical judgment—we must cultivate a
radical democratic pedagogy of everyday life, one that nurtures the civic
imagination, deepens historical consciousness, and expands the capacities
necessary for self-government. Such a pedagogy teaches people not only how to
recognize domination but also how to imagine, create, and sustain the
democratic socialist society capable of transforming freedom, equality, and
solidarity from abstract ideals into the lived conditions of a just and
flourishing democracy.
